Overall a good oven but some flaws with control board and company doesn't help troubleshoot - I ran into a known issue with this stove above 4 years after I bought it, which is that moisture got under the keypad and it started beeping and giving me an error constantly. I couldn't even use the stove because anytime it was plugged in, it was beeping so much.

the company was not helpful; they just wanted to send a repair guy out, which is 80$ just to come out plus prbly 350-500 to replace the control board.

All you need to do is to peel the cover off and gently clean the contacts below with alcohol and q-tips. There are many youtube videos of how to fix this.

Also, even if you need your control board replaced, it looks very simple (unscrew the back of the stove, plug and play to put the new one in). So check out those options before paying for an expensive repair.

The stove is great otherwise. I'm annoyed that frigidaire a) doesn't have any kind of sealant around the keyboard cover to prevent this common, known issue and b) doesn't provide troubleshooting to help you fix the problem yourself. Also, although frigidaire's customer service did eventually give me the parts numbers (which I wanted in case we did need to replace teh control board), I had to ask them several times and they kept trying to push me to hire a repair guy instead. I finally said "Am I allowed to know the parts numbers?" and then they gave it to me. I wonder if they get a kickback from the repair costs, since they were so pushy about it.

Shouldn't cost a lotta money to fix this, and I"m sure a lot of people pay way too much for the repair.

Quick and easy fix - These "agitator dogs" were a perfect fit for the worn out parts in my 17 year old Sears Kenmore Series 80 washing machine, Model # 110.25842400. Ok. Ish - So I bought a new Keurig at Christmas. Multi stream. Way cool. Only, my reusable k cups no longer work. So, I bought one of these schmancy ones to try. Of note, my husband and I use the disposable k cups for some coffees. So, every time I used the keurig brand reusable k cup….

1. Remove the piece from the machine that holds the disposable k cup.
2. Take the lid off of the reusable k cup.
3. Remove the part that holds the coffee and fill it.
4. Drop a disposable k filter into the holder for the coffee holder. (Without this, too much grit ended up in my coffee and I couldn’t drink the last inch of the cup.)
5. Drop the part with the coffee in and try to remember how to put the lids on.
6. Insert the k cup reusable unit into the hole vacated in step one.
7. After brewing, try to figure out how to take it all apart and empty it out, clean it, etc.

As a friend gives me free Starbucks beans, it was cheaper than buying disposable, but ugh. What a process. I found a different brand that works just as well that requires fewer steps. This was a poorly designed product!

the posts are labeled on the back so you can easily identify the wiring setup. i thought about soldering my wires on, but opted instead for these [[ASIN:B00030CSZC quick connect blade terminals]] so i can easily disassemble the project when making changes. for the price, these connectors are a no-brainer!

I didn't need this, but . . . - Lint builds up over the years in the dryer vent and can either start mucking up your drying cycle or even catch fire if it gets too hot. You should clean the duct every 2-3 years as part of your household routine.

I only have a short run of aluminum flex duct feeding to an outside wall, so it would have been just as easy to replace the duct with a new one. If you have a hard pipe that feeds up the walls, however, you really NEED this Deflector Dryer Duct Cleaning Kit or similar.

This solidly-made kit extends up to 12-feet with six soft fiberglass sections tipped with steel threads and a fat, soft brush head. You can just shove it down the duct by hand or use an electric drill to spin clean the duct with a clockwise spin. (NOTE: you MUST use clockwise--counterclockwise will unscrew the sections!) The long, soft fiberglass sections sorta flop sideways all over the place when using a drill, so you might need to slowly feed it in a section at a time. When I finished, I also used a blower to blast out the last of the lingering dust.

NOTE: Don't tear up the package it ships in--just pull out the staples. When finished you can easily repack and store the tough package on the wall.

NOTE 2: You might be able to use this kit to clean refrigerator coils. They also need to be cleaned every 2-3 years for proper operation and cooling efficiency.

This is a solid five-star cleaning kit.
